subject: Agriculture
title: The Organic Yield Gap
description: A quick, practical guide to The Organic Yield Gap.

hook.text: Organic farms typically produce 20% less per hectare than conventional farms. Critics say we can't afford that gap.

buildup.text: The gap varies wildly—5% for some crops, 40% for others. It depends on crop, location, and management skill.

discovery.text: Meta-analyses show the gap shrinks with good management. Diversified organic systems nearly match conventional.

twist.text: If food waste and overconsumption were reduced, the organic yield gap would be irrelevant to global food supply.

climax.text: The real question isn't yield per hectare—it's total system output including environmental costs.

punchline.text: 20% less yield. 100% less pollution. Which number matters more?

quiz.question: What is the typical organic yield gap compared to conventional farming?
options: About 20% less on average, varying by crop

details.summary: The organic yield gap is the difference in crop output between organic and conventional farming, typically ranging from 10 to 25 percent less for organic. This topic explores the causes, variability, and debate over whether organic farming can scale to feed the world.
details.whyItMatters: The yield gap is the central challenge in the argument for scaling organic agriculture. Understanding its causes and variability is key to evaluating whether organic farming is a viable path for global food security.
takeaways: Organic yields are typically 10-25% lower than conventional depending on the crop
The gap narrows significantly for legumes, perennials, and in drought conditions
Better organic management practices can close much of the yield gap over time

faq.question: Why do organic farms typically produce less than conventional farms?
faq.answer: Organic farms cannot use synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, which provide a rapid nutrient boost, or synthetic pesticides that control weeds and pests more aggressively. Nutrient cycling and biological pest control are effective but slower-acting, resulting in somewhat lower yields.

faq.question: Can the organic yield gap be closed?
faq.answer: Research shows the gap narrows significantly with improved soil management, diverse crop rotations, and polyculture systems. For some crops like legumes and fruits, well-managed organic farms already match conventional yields, especially over long time horizons.
